with the great apostasy? Hey, thank you
for a great question. And there are a
handful of passages that contribute to
this notion that there was going to be a
rebellion or a falling away or an
apostasy that would precede Jesus's
second coming. And you see it primarily
in like 2 Thessalonians 2:3, but also in
1 Timothy 4 and in 2 Timothy 3 and
perhaps even in Matthew 20. Now all of
these passages are being written toward
the end of the 1st century CE or the
beginning of the 2 century CE. The
passages that are attributed to Paul are
not actually coming from Paul. First and
second Timothy were written decades
after Paul's death. And second
Thessalonians was probably also
pseudapographic, not actually written by
Paul, but written by somebody pretending
to be Paul after his death. And the
point of these passages is probably to
account for the fact that Jesus hadn't
come back yet. That they were expecting
him to come back within that first
generation after Jesus's death. And that
didn't happen. They've got to make sense
of why Jesus is not coming back. And
this idea develops that, oh well, it
turns out people are abandoning the
faith. People are falling away. Jesus
can't come back until this falling away
takes place. And so it's a way to
explain the delayed perusia, the delayed
second coming of Jesus. And then that
later gets picked up by groups that want
to challenge the priesthood authority of
the Catholic Church, particularly the
LDS church. Uh the Mormon church
structures its own power and authority
by suggesting that the priesthood power
was taken from the earth shortly after
Jesus's death and resurrection. And the
LDS church is there to restore it. and
some Protestants also will appeal to
this to challenge the authority of the
Catholic Church. So there are a variety
of ways that the story can get picked up
by contemporary religious communities.
But when these texts were originally
written, the idea was probably to make
